narrative:
The model estimated a 56.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. Because that is above a 50% failure risk, your law school application was rejected. This is a risk estimate, not a judgment of your ability, but it means the model found more evidence pointing toward failure than toward passing.

The strongest factor was your part-time status. Accepted applicants were overwhelmingly full-time, and your part-time plan was the single most important factor pushing the prediction toward failure. The second strongest factor was your third-year class standing: you were in the third decile, compared with an accepted-student average around the sixth decile, and this also pushed toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA, 2.70 versus 3.23 for accepted students, was the third most important factor, but in this prediction it pushed slightly toward passing—it acted as a modest counterweight, not the main reason for denial.

To improve future chances, ask admissions for feedback, consider a full-time study plan or reducing work hours, and address your third-year academic standing directly. You may also strengthen your LSAT and academic record and provide evidence of improved performance before reapplying.
